title: Study Finds Greatest Predictors of Good Reading Skills
paragraphs: Teachers know — and researchers have confirmed — that good literacy skills can really help a child when they're trying to learn a second language.
This is because the reading and writing skills they learn in their first language carry over into any new languages they learn.
And one study published in Journal of Intelligence has now challenged some common beliefs about what makes a child a good reader.

According to the researchers at Texas A&M University, many people believe that smart kids just read well, while kids who aren't as smart don't. And some children who have problems with reading must have issues with visual processing and how they see text.
However, the researchers looked at a wide range of cognitive and achievement tests to look at nearly 50,000 possible relationships between different types of cognitive abilities and reading results.
And they found that people's common beliefs about reading aren't really right.

The researchers did find that general intelligence matters to reading, but far less than older research suggested. And, perhaps most surprisingly, visual processing showed no real relationship with reading skills.
Instead, auditory processing — being able to hear and decode the sounds in words — was found to have a far greater effect on reading skills.
Something known as "comprehension-knowledge" also turned out to be important for reading. This refers to all the ideas, words and background knowledge children build up from the world around them.
In fact, these two skills were the greatest predictors of reading ability among children. Memory, mental processing speed and reasoning also played important roles.
These findings could give both teachers and parents better ways to support children with reading.
"Strengthening foundational skills at home, even the ones that seem simple, can have meaningful effects on more advanced reading abilities," said researcher Daniel Hajovsky.
